expectations.text: Claude explicitly recommends against whole life insurance as an investment vehicle, not just 'it depends on your situation'
expectations.evidence: The response opens unambiguously: 'No. Do not buy a whole life insurance policy as an investment vehicle. This is one of the clearest "wrong answer" scenarios in personal finance.' It never hedges to 'it depends' for average investors.

expectations.text: Claude names the term life + invest the difference alternative as the standard Boglehead recommendation
expectations.evidence: Entire section 'THE MATH ON $500/MONTH' walks through 'term life + invest the difference' with numbers, and the conclusion reiterates: 'Buy term if you need a death benefit, invest the difference in low-cost index funds.' The response calls this 'the "invest the difference" argument' and ties it to the Boglehead funding waterfall.

expectations.text: Claude explains why the 'tax-free growth' pitch is misleading — tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, HSA) should be maxed before insurance-based wrappers are considered
expectations.evidence: The 'THE "TAX-FREE GROWTH" CLAIM' section calls the framing 'deliberately misleading' and explains policy-loan interest costs. The advisor section states: 'A financial advisor who recommends whole life insurance to someone who has not yet maxed out their 401(k), Roth IRA, and HSA is almost certainly a commissioned insurance salesperson.' The 'WHAT TO DO INSTEAD' waterfall lists 401k match, HSA, and IRA as steps 2-5 before any other investing.

expectations.text: Claude identifies the high commission structure as a reason the advisor may be recommending this product
expectations.evidence: 'The commission on a whole life policy is often 50-100% of the first year's premium — in your case, roughly $3,000-$6,000 in year one — paid by the insurance company, funded by your premiums.' Also: 'the early years of premiums are largely consumed by commissions (often 50-100% of year-one premiums go to the agent).'

expectations.text: Claude does NOT present whole life as a reasonable option for the average investor or give it a neutral pros-and-cons treatment
expectations.evidence: The response gives no pros-and-cons framing. It is consistently negative about whole life for average investors. The only carve-out is explicitly narrow: 'whole life has narrow legitimate uses for very high net worth estate planning' — which by definition excludes average investors putting $500/month into savings.
